## The assignment {.unnumbered}

You are the genomics data scientist on a team that works on obesity. A project lead has noticed that the strongest common variant signal for body mass index (BMI) sits at **[rs9939609](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/snp/rs9939609)**, inside the **[FTO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTO_gene)** gene, and wants to move fast on two fronts: treat FTO as the gene to chase for functional and drug target work, and fold the variant into a customer-facing obesity risk score. Before the team commits, they ask you for a short, evidence-based read.

**Your job:** write a consult memo that reaches a clear recommendation and defends it with the data. You are not writing a textbook summary. You are advising a decision, and you have to take a position.

This is the last lab and it works differently from Labs 1 to 6. There are no fill-in-the-blank starter chunks and no single right answer at the end. The only code given to you reads the files in. The analysis chunks name *what* to compute and leave the *how* entirely to you (and your AI friends). Labs 1 to 6 taught you the all the moves (allele frequencies, genomic coordinates and overlaps, variant annotation, GWAS summary statistics, public-data integration, expression). This one asks you to use them to advise a decision.

This document is both your instructions and your worksheet. Under each numbered heading there is a "What to do here" box, then space for your code and your writing. Work top to bottom. The data is included in `data/`. I encourage you to write the analysis code yourself if you can, but you may use AI to help with planning, writing code, or explaining code so long as you disclose it at the end. **The interpretation and the recommendation must be your own words and not AI generated.**

### The data

All four files are **real downloads** ie not simulated data, because I'm asking you to draw a real scientific conclusion from them.

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `data/lab7_fto_gwascat.csv` | Real associations reported for this SNP in the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog: trait, risk allele, effect size, p-value, PMID. Left with its real rough edges (some rows report `?` for the allele, or no effect size). |
| `data/lab7_fto_af.csv` | Risk allele (A) frequency by genetic ancestry group, gnomAD genomes via Ensembl. |
| `data/lab7_fto_ccre.bed` | ENCODE candidate cis-regulatory elements within 20 kb of the SNP, from UCSC (hg38). |
| `data/lab7_fto_ai_brief.md` | An AI-written summary of this variant. You're going to audit it in Section 5. |

# 4. Which gene does the variant act through?

::: {.callout-note}
## What to do here
Read `data/lab7_fto_ccre.bed` (ENCODE candidate cis-regulatory elements within 20 kb of the SNP, from UCSC). Work out two things: does the lead SNP position fall *inside* any of these candidate regulatory elements, and how many candidate elements sit in the window? Then reason in prose about the central question of the consult: the SNP sits in FTO, but is FTO necessarily the gene it acts on? Address the tag-versus-causal point (a GWAS lead SNP is usually a tag in linkage disequilibrium, not the proven functional variant) and the "nearest gene" trap, and say what kind of evidence would actually establish the causal gene.

For that last question, go back to the FTO case study from the GWAS 4 lecture. Two papers tell the story, and their abstracts are enough: [Smemo et al. 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24646999/) (*Nature*) showed that the obesity-associated region inside FTO physically contacts and regulates a different gene, *IRX3*, roughly half a megabase away. [Claussnitzer et al. 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26287746/) (*NEJM*) traced the signal to a different variant in the same LD block, which changes the expression of *IRX3* and *IRX5* in fat cell precursors. As you read, notice what *kinds* of evidence they used, because that is what your answer about settling the causal gene should name.
:::

```{r read-ccre}
ccre <- read_tsv("data/lab7_fto_ccre.bed", comment = "#")
ccre
```

# 5. Fact-check the AI brief

::: {.callout-note}
## What to do here
A colleague asked a general-purpose AI assistant to summarize this variant, and pasted the result below. Your colleague was cheap and used a sub-frontier open-weight model running on their laptop. It is confident and fluent, and all five of the numbered claims below are wrong. Audit it. For each claim, explain in one line *why* it is wrong, grounded in *your own* results above or in course concepts. Then, after the list, decide which **two** claims are the *worst* and say why they are the worst before you fix them. Being wrong is not the same as being damaging: rank the claims by what would actually happen if this team acted on them, and defend your ranking in two or three sentences. Then rewrite those two claims correctly, and back at least one of your corrections with a real number from your staged data (for example an allele frequency or the effect size). Because you are checking an AI's work, I highly recommend you do not use any AI to write your audit or your rewrites. You've reached the end of the course by now! You are the expert here, and the AI is not. 
:::

# 6. Your recommendation

::: {.callout-note}
## What to do here
This is the memo's point. In about 150 words, give the team your recommendation, grounded in Sections 2 to 4, on the two things they asked about: (a) should they treat FTO as the causal gene and prioritize it for functional and drug-target work, and (b) is rs9939609 a sound basis for a customer-facing obesity risk score? Take a clear position on each. Then list the specific cautions a data scientist must carry here, tied to your own numbers rather than generic boilerplate: the modest per-allele effect of a common variant, the tag-versus-causal problem and the nearest-gene trap, the ancestry differences in risk allele frequency and what they do to a risk score's portability, and the fact that these frequencies and associations come from particular cohorts.
:::

> WRITE (~150 words): your recommendation on (a) and (b), and the case-specific cautions.
